title: When aid becomes a weapon, children lose more than food
subtitle: A new analysis finds a sixteenfold rise in verified aid-denial incidents over a decade. The consequences reach children’s water, healthcare and schooling—and demand scrutiny of who stops help reaching them.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Save the Children warned on 18 November that denying children humanitarian assistance has become an increasingly common tactic of war, publishing an analysis that puts verified access-denial incidents at more than sixteen times their level a decade earlier.

Its report, Access Restricted: Delivering Aid Against the Odds, compares 509 incidents in 2015 with 8,322 verified in 2025. The warning concerns the systems that keep children alive: permission for a convoy to move, protection for its driver, and the ability of a clinic to receive what it needs.
What the figures measure

The United Nations independently reports the 8,322 figure in its monitoring of children and armed conflict. Denial of humanitarian access is one of the six grave violations covered by that system; it includes attacks on humanitarian personnel as well as obstruction of assistance.

These are incidents, not a count of individual children. Nor is the figure a complete census of deprivation worldwide. The UN says its 2025 verification work includes violations committed in earlier years. Restricted access also makes abuses harder to document. The comparison therefore shows a sharp rise in verified incidents, without measuring every obstruction or establishing how many children each affected.

Save the Children says the occupied Palestinian territory, Libya and Ukraine together accounted for about 90 per cent of the total. That concentration matters: a global headline does not mean the same increase occurred in every conflict. The organisation is both an aid provider and an advocate, publishing the analysis alongside a fundraising campaign.
The risk goes beyond an empty food parcel

Humanitarian assistance is also drinking water, sanitation, healthcare, education and protection. UNICEF’s current emergency appeal treats these as connected services for children and their caregivers. Getting food across a border cannot, by itself, restore the conditions in which a child can safely eat, recover from illness and attend school.

UNICEF’s Water Under Fire report, released on 5 November, illustrates that connection. Covering attacks affecting water systems, workers and users in 23 countries and territories between January 2021 and June 2026, it describes restrictions on treatment chemicals and spare parts alongside physical destruction. The agency warns that damaged water services increase risks of disease, malnutrition and violence.

For a family, the consequences can arrive together. In its 13 November Gaza update, the UN humanitarian office, OCHA, reported sewage-contaminated floodwater, disrupted health services and medicine shortages. Rain had also damaged more than 100 learning spaces and 15 child and psychosocial spaces, as well as a safe space serving women and girls. OCHA said Israeli restrictions and funding shortfalls were constraining the response.

Those are different causes requiring different remedies. A donation can help purchase supplies; it cannot itself secure permission to move them. Equally, an approved shipment cannot reach a family if the organisation lacks the money or transport to deliver it.
Permission is not the same as delivery

OCHA’s account shows why headline truck totals need scrutiny. It reported that 228 UN and partner trucks were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom between 2 and 8 November, around 42 per cent fewer than the previous week. It attributed the decline mainly to Israel’s suspension of the Egyptian corridor, reportedly over smuggling concerns, while also identifying reduced aid volumes linked to funding constraints.

Israel disputes accounts that place primary responsibility for shortages on its policies. In a statement published on 6 November, the Israeli military and its aid-coordination agency, COGAT, described winter-supply approvals and said equipment covered by roughly half of approved requests had not yet entered Gaza, partly because of logistical and budgetary difficulties unrelated to Israel. The military also accused Hamas of exploiting humanitarian aid. These were its published positions before the new Save the Children analysis, not a response obtained by ATHENA.

The competing accounts make independent tracking essential: what was requested, what was approved, why movement stopped, and what actually reached households. Permission, border offloading and distribution are separate stages.
Security controls have limits

International humanitarian law allows parties to inspect relief consignments and regulate routes and timing, the International Committee of the Red Cross explains. But those controls must not unduly delay assistance or make its delivery impossible. Parties must facilitate relief for civilians in need, including people living in territory controlled by an enemy.

Calling a restriction “weaponisation” is an allegation about how power is being used. Establishing responsibility for a particular violation requires evidence about the conduct and circumstances; a shortfall alone does not establish deliberate deprivation. Security language, however, does not remove the obligation to protect civilians and facilitate aid.

For ATHENA, the measure of success is whether children receive help safely and consistently, and whether their families and the workers supporting them can challenge the barriers. Children’s survival should not depend on which armed actor controls the road to their clinic or the border through which their medicine must pass.
The Athena Perspective.
